vyasanamaṇusaṃcayasamarthane | kiṃca avayavinaṃ dūṣayitumaṇusaṃcayamātravastuvādinā yadabhyadhāyi ghaṭasya ekatra pārśve chāyā, paratra ātapaḥ, madhyabhāgaḥ pārśvadvayena āvṛtaḥ, pārśvadvayamanāvṛtam, ataśca tathābhūtāvayavaviśrāntaśarīro'vayavī yugapadeva viruddhāṃ chāyāṃ kathaṃ kṣamatāmātapasaṃyuktaśca na ca iti, āvṛtaśca naca iti ca | āvaraṇena raktādayo'pi upalakṣyante | citratantau bhāgo raktaḥ, aṃśāntaramaraktaṃ, bhāgāntaramasitamanyat pītamityādi | tasmāt vastutvasya vyāpakaṃ viruddhadharmasaṃbandhavandhyatvaṃ yat, tadviruddhasya viruddhadharmasaṃsargasya upalabdhyā vastutvaniṣedho'vayavinaḥ,- iti tatparamāṇāvapi samānam | pārśvadvaye hi madhyaparamāṇoryadi paramāṇudvayaṃ, tadā prāgvṛttitayā sūryasaṃmukhasya aṇorātapayogaḥ, pratyagvṛttestu tadayogaḥ, madhyavartinaśca dvābhyāmāvaraṇamiti ghaṭate | yāvatā madhyavartino nirbhāgasya pārśvadvaye sati madhyavartitvānupapattiḥ, iti paramāṇutrayādārabhya (page 144) sthūlaghaṭādiparyante vastuni cchāyātapavibhāga āvṛtānāvṛtatvaraktāraktādirviśeṣo ya upalabhyate, so'ṇusaṃcayavāde nirvivādasiddha iti yaduktam, taduktisārameva, na yuktisāramaṇoḥ sāṃśatvena vinā asya vidherayogāt, niraṃśasyaiva vā pārśvadvayādiyoge taddeśatvātaddeśatvavaiśasāpattiḥ | aṃśadvayamaye asya ekatve avayavivādasyaiva abhyupagamaprasaṅgaḥ | aṃśasya aṇutvāṃśāntaraparyanuyogena pralayāntarāpātaḥ | kiṃca cchāyālokanīlapītādiparamāṇusaṃcaye viśvatra bhāvāvacchedāvadherayogaḥ vijātīyatayā avacchede citre ekatvena kathaṃ pratītiḥ, vastuto madhyapūrvāparatādyabhāve niyamābhāvāt saṃniveśabhedapratyayaḥ kathamityādayo deṣāḥ | etadupasaṃharati vijñānavādibhiḥ iti | ālambanaparīkṣādau daiṅgāge, vijñaptimātrādisiddhāvāsabandhanyāṃ, prajñālaṃkārādiṣu bhāṭṭadarśaneṣu, tatra tatra ca anyatra vitatya ayamartha ukta iti | ayaṃ bhāvaḥ- dūṣaṇakalāpena anena viṣayasya asattvamāvedayatā bāhyārthaviṣayaṃ yat pramāṇaṃ pareṇa pratyakṣaṃ samabhāvyata, tadasamarthatayā pramāṇābhāsīkartavyam | tato niṣpramāṇako bāhyo'rthaḥ kathaṃ sidhyet,
**The Lord creates from within, like a yogin** The external object has been demolished. The whole (avayavin) cannot stand: a jar has shadow on one side and sun on the other, its middle covered and its sides uncovered — so the one whole that was to bear all these contradictory states is impossible. And the atom (paramāṇu) fares no better: the middle atom, being part-less, cannot have two sides, one sun-lit and one shaded; the two-part atom collapses back into the whole it was meant to replace; and the parts run on to infinity. Whether the Buddhist posits a whole or atoms, the external thing has no valid means behind it. It cannot be established. But then the objector asks a fair question: "You yourself established the external by the variety of the appearance-order, as its cause. So how is it un-established now?" And this is where Abhinavagupta turns from destruction to construction. The external is not needed, because the Lord manifests the whole world from within himself, by his own will, without any external material cause — exactly as a yogin does. Consider what has been granted on all sides. The consciousness-form is the locus in which objects are established; and by its power of synthesis it is one. Its lordship — its very God-ness — is the freedom to join and separate the appearances. And the objects are, in their being, the manifestation of this consciousness. So the whole world is, from the first, *within* the consciousness — the inner-containing- world-form. And with this freedom there must be the will: the un-thwarted will, whose very nature is freedom. And that the will creates — without any external cause — is already seen in the dream. In the dream, the jar appears, and the whole clay-wheel-stick-lineage of causes is absent. The dream proves that the consciousness alone can create an object-mass, by its will, without a material cause. The objection: "then the jar is unreal." Let it be so, Abhinavagupta answers — and still the point holds. For the yogin creates an army, a city, by the mere will. If someone says "the atoms are joined by the will, as the material cause," then if the whole known cause-complement (the clay, the wheel, the helpers) were accepted, the yogin would be just a potter. But when he transcends the known — creates with even a straw — the dream and the construction show that the consciousness's power to bring about the being-appearance needs no external cause at all. As the verse has it: "no other cause of the dream's object-variety is seen than your manifestation-power; being seen to have that power, it alone is the one cause of the whole world's manifestation." And even the yogin — whose consciousness is tinted by body and breath — is, by its purity, a creator; so how much more the pure consciousness-tattva, which everywhere is the creator. The God, the consciousness-self, manifests the whole object-mass from within himself, by his will, like a yogin, without any external material cause. This is the īśvarādvaya — the non-dual lordship. The world is not made from a stuff outside the Lord; it is his own inner being, manifested outward by his will. And this is why the external object was never needed: not because the world is unreal, but because its reality is the Lord's own manifestation, arising from within, by the freedom of his will. ---

> The external object has been shown to be un-establishable — neither as a whole nor as atoms. The > objector asks how this is so, since the external was earlier inferred from the variety of the > appearance-order. Abhinavagupta answers with the īśvarādvaya: the external is not needed, because the > Lord manifests the whole world from within himself, by his own will, without an external material > cause — as a yogin does. The decisive image is the dream. The Buddhist had used the dream to prove the > world's unreality (it appears without a cause). Abhinavagupta accepts that the dream is uncaused, but > draws the opposite conclusion: the dream shows that consciousness alone can create an object-mass by > its will. > > The passage establishes the īśvarādvaya — the Lord manifests from within. Whether this yields one > universal creator, rather than a creating consciousness, is a further claim addressed later. (the Buddhist's example, re-read) · avayavin/paramāṇu (whole/atom).
